steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: In October 1918, Germany was facing defeat in World War I. The Kaiser's government transformed into a parliamentary democracy to secure better peace terms. However, the revolution went further than intended when sailors mutinied at Kiel on 3 November 1918.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The Weimar Constitution, approved on 11 August 1919, created the most democratic system Germany had ever known - but it contained crucial weaknesses that opponents exploited.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Friedrich Ebert, leader of the SPD, became the first President of the Weimar Republic in February 1919. He governed using Article 48 136 times during his presidency (1919-1925), often to deal with political crises - setting a dangerous precedent for future use.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: In January 1919, the Communist Spartacist League (led by Rosa Luxemburg and Karl Liebknecht) attempted to overthrow the Weimar government in Berlin. The government used the Freikorps (right-wing ex-soldiers) to crush the uprising. Luxemburg and Liebknecht were murdered on 15 January 1919.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Describe two weaknesses of the Weimar Constitution. (4 marks) | Explain why the Spartacist Uprising failed. (8 marks) | How far was the Weimar Republic threatened by right-wing opposition in the years 1919-1923? (12 marks)

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: For questions about the Constitution, always discuss both strengths AND weaknesses - examiners want balance Use precise dates: Kaiser abdicated 9 November 1918; Constitution approved 11 August 1919; Spartacist Uprising January 1919; Kapp Putsch March 1920 When comparing left and right threats, use the statistics: 354 right-wing murders vs 22 left-wing; average sentences 4 months vs 15 years Article 48 is the single most important constitutional weakness - make sure you can explain exactly how it was used and abused The "stab-in-the-back" myth is crucial for explaining why the Republic lacked legitimacy from the start Always link political events to consequences: the Spartacist Uprising led to the SPD-KPD split, which later prevented anti-Nazi unity
